nodes.summary: Let $w$ be the free resource vector and let the list of pending processes contain no duplicates. The detection algorithm, started with $w$ free, reports no process if and only if some reordering of the pending processes is a reduction sequence from $w$.
nodes.title: No deadlock is reported exactly when all the processes can finish

nodes.summary: Let $w$ be the free resource vector. For every process $q$ that the detection algorithm reports, the request of $q$ is not at most $w$ plus the sum of the allocations of the processes that the algorithm lets finish: for at least one resource type, $q$ requests more than is free even after all those processes have released their allocations.
nodes.title: Every reported process is stuck

nodes.summary: Given the free resource vector $w$ and a list of pending processes, repeatedly take the first pending process whose request is at most what is free, let it finish, remove that entry from the list and add its allocation to what is free, until no pending process has a request at most what is free. The processes still pending then are the ones reported as deadlocked.
nodes.title: The detection algorithm

nodes.summary: Let $w$ be a resource vector. If $\sigma$ is a reduction sequence from $w$ and no process of $\sigma$ has a request at most $w$, then $\sigma$ is empty.
nodes.title: A reduction sequence in which no process fits is empty

nodes.summary: Let $w$ be a resource vector and $p$ a process whose request is at most $w$. If $\sigma$ is a reduction sequence from $w$, then the list obtained from $\sigma$ by removing the first occurrence of $p$, if any, is a reduction sequence from $w$ plus the allocation of $p$.
nodes.title: Letting a process that fits finish first preserves reduction sequences

nodes.summary: For every free resource vector $w$ and every list of pending processes, the processes that the detection algorithm lets finish, in the order it lets them finish, form a reduction sequence from $w$.
nodes.title: The processes the algorithm lets finish form a reduction sequence

nodes.summary: Given the free resource vector $w$ and a list of pending processes, run the detection algorithm: repeatedly take the first pending process whose request is at most what is free, let it finish, remove that entry from the list and add its allocation to what is free, until no pending process has a request at most what is free. This is the list of the processes taken, in the order they were taken.
nodes.title: The processes the detection algorithm lets finish

nodes.summary: Let $w$ be the free resource vector and let the list of pending processes contain no duplicates. A process $p$ is reported by the detection algorithm if and only if $p$ is pending and no duplicate-free reduction sequence $\sigma$ from $w$ made of pending processes contains $p$.
nodes.title: Correctness of deadlock detection

nodes.summary: Let $w$ be the free resource vector, let the list of pending processes contain no duplicates, and let the fuel be at least the number of pending processes. If $\sigma$ is a duplicate-free reduction sequence from $w$ all of whose processes are pending, then no process of $\sigma$ is among the processes that the detection algorithm with that fuel leaves over.
nodes.title: The algorithm with fuel leaves over no process of a reduction sequence

nodes.summary: Given the fuel, a number of steps, together with the free resource vector $w$ and a list of pending processes, the algorithm returns two lists: the processes that finished, in order, and the processes left over. With fuel $0$, or when no pending process has a request at most $w$, no process finishes and all the pending processes are left over. Otherwise the fuel is $n + 1$ for some $n$; take the first pending…
nodes.title: The detection algorithm with fuel

nodes.summary: Let $P$ be a type of processes and $R$ a type of resource types, and let $S$ be a state that gives each process $p$ an allocation $\mathrm{alloc}(p)$ and a request $\mathrm{request}(p)$, both functions $R \to \mathbb{N}$ ordered componentwise. A list of processes $p_1, \dots, p_k$ is a reduction sequence of $S$ from the free vector $w : R \to \mathbb{N}$ when, for every $1 \le i \le k$, we have…
nodes.title: Reduction sequences

nodes.summary: For a type $P$ of processes and a type $R$ of resource types, a state consists of two functions $\mathrm{alloc}, \mathrm{request} : P \to R \to \mathbb{N}$: $\mathrm{alloc}(p)(r)$ is the number of instances of resource type $r$ that process $p$ holds, and $\mathrm{request}(p)(r)$ is the number of instances of $r$ that $p$ is waiting for.
nodes.title: Resource-allocation state

can_prove.label: ready to prove
can_prove.meaning: Statement is in Lean and nothing it needs is blocked, so the proof can start.

can_state.label: ready to state
can_state.meaning: Everything its statement uses is in Lean, so the statement can be written in Lean.

conditional.label: conditionally proved
conditional.meaning: Proof compiles, but rests on an open statement without a recorded Lean proof.

fully_proved.label: fully proved
fully_proved.meaning: Proved, and every prerequisite is fully proved too.

inventory_checked.label: inventory checked
inventory_checked.meaning: Module inventory checked in full; it records inspection, not a mathematical proof.

inventory_pending.label: inventory pending
inventory_pending.meaning: Module inventory not yet checked in full; it records inspection, not a mathematical proof.

not_ready.label: not ready
not_ready.meaning: Needs more blueprint work before it can be attempted.

proved.label: proved
proved.meaning: Proof compiles, but something it rests on is not finished.

stated.label: statement formalized
stated.meaning: Statement is in Lean; the proof is not.
